blocks.text: Stimulation lifts normal to high; antidepressant lifts low to high.

Stimulation is a class of drug effect that pushes the activity level of the central nervous system upward. Drugs that produce it are called stimulants. It isn't the same thing as an antidepressant: an antidepressant pulls a low person back to normal, a stimulant pushes a normal person up to high.
By structure, a stimulant is either amphetamine-class or it isn't.

items: Amphetamine class: amphetamine, methamphetamine, cathinones. Strong effect, strong risk; the source text mentioned a 2017 case in the US where someone on bath salts (a cathinone derivative) went out into the street and bit a homeless man.
Non-phenethylamine class: cocaine, caffeine, and the SRIs pushed into this class pharmacologically.

blocks.text: By effect, the specific entries separate 'stimulation' from 'antidepressant' again: stimulation lifts normal to high, antidepressant lifts low to high. The two classifications use different axes; there's no need to force them together.

Stimulants push heart rate, blood pressure, pupils and body temperature up together, while pushing appetite and sleepiness down. Short term it looks like 'better energy'; long term it's tolerance, withdrawal and cardiovascular risk.

items: Tolerance: the same amount does less and less.
Withdrawal: the effect passes, arousal rebounds, and drowsiness, depression and anxiety come back together.
Cardiovascular: faster heartbeat, higher blood pressure; especially dangerous for people with underlying conditions.
Neurotoxicity: long-term amphetamine use can bring paranoia, hallucinations, stimulant psychosis.

blocks.text: Caffeine is the most common stimulant, and the one least treated as a 'drug'.

It pushes drowsiness away, but adenosine keeps piling up; when the effect passes, the sleepiness comes back all at once. In report 7 caffeine appears repeatedly as a supporting player to dextromethorphan: sometimes to stay awake, sometimes just as daily habit. It doesn't change the direction of dissociation; it only raises the person's arousal a little.

Caffeine tolerance comes fast: the same amount wakes you less; stop it and adenosine piles up, and headache, drowsiness and scattered attention come back together. It's the mildest stimulant, and the one most easily ignored.

Ephedrine is a common ingredient in asthma medicine, and it's a stimulant. Its blood-pressure risk is high; stacked with certain drugs, the risk isn't additive. The source text recorded a fatal combination once in report 74; this entry doesn't expand that combination, and keeps only the conclusion: ephedrine isn't 'naturally safe'.

Pregabalin may make a person feel lively, and can even be mistaken for a stimulant; but its mechanism contradicts the definition of a stimulant. In ODW it goes under sedation/anxiolytic, not stimulation. Looking only at how it feels and not at the mechanism is the easiest mistake in classification.
Stimulants push normal people toward abnormal; antidepressants pull abnormal people back to normal.
